# AMC 20-115D — Airborne Software Development Assurance Using EUROCAE ED-12 and RTCA DO-178

> [!summary]
> AMC 20-115D is the software route. It recognises EUROCAE ED-12C and RTCA
> DO-178C, their four supplements and the tool qualification document, as an
> acceptable means for the software aspects of airborne systems and equipment.
> Almost all of the substance sits inside those documents, which their
> publishers sell and which this vault does not hold. What the AMC itself
> carries is the acceptance, the rules for legacy software and tools, and one
> EASA precedence rule. This note records that and stops.

## Requirement

The verbs are AMC 20-115D's own. It is an acceptable means of compliance, so
"should" marks an accepted method and an applicant may propose an alternative
and justify it.

### What the AMC accepts, sections 1 to 3

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **1.a** | The AMC describes an acceptable means, but not the only means, for showing compliance with the applicable airworthiness regulations with regard to the software aspects of airborne systems and equipment, in the domain of product certification or ETSO authorisation. | Statement |
| **1.a** | Compliance with the AMC is not mandatory, and an applicant may elect to use an alternative means of compliance. | Permitted |
| **1.a** | An alternative means of compliance must meet the relevant requirements, ensure "an equivalent level of software safety as this AMC", and be approved by EASA on a product or ETSO article basis. | Required |
| **1.b** | The AMC recognises EUROCAE ED-12C and RTCA DO-178C, Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification, dated 1 January 2012 and 13 December 2011; ED-215 and DO-330 on software tool qualification; ED-216 and DO-333, the formal methods supplement; ED-217 and DO-332, the object-oriented technology supplement; and ED-218 and DO-331, the model-based development and verification supplement. | Statement |
| **1.b** | Where the notation ED-XXX/DO-XXX appears, the two referenced documents are recognised as being equivalent. | Statement |
| **1.c** | ED-94C and DO-248C are identified as supporting documents. They contain frequently asked questions and discussion papers, compiled and approved by the authors of ED-12C and DO-178C, that clarify the guidance in ED-12C/DO-178C. | Statement |
| **1.d** | A reference to the use of ED-12C/DO-178C in the AMC includes the use of ED-215/DO-330 and of the supplements ED-216/DO-333, ED-217/DO-332 and ED-218/DO-331, as applicable. | Statement |
| **1.e** | The AMC establishes guidance for using existing ED-12B/DO-178B processes for new software development. | Statement |
| **1.f** | The AMC also establishes guidance for transitioning to ED-12C/DO-178C when making modifications to software previously approved using ED-12/DO-178, ED-12A/DO-178A or ED-12B/DO-178B. | Statement |
| **2** | The AMC applies to applicants, design approval holders and developers of airborne systems and equipment containing software to be installed on type-certified aircraft, engines and propellers, or to be used in ETSO articles. | Statement |
| **3** | The AMC replaces and cancels AMC 20-115C, Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification, 12 September 2013. | Statement |
| **4.a** | Appendix A, Section 3 of ED-12C/DO-178C summarises the differences between ED-12C/DO-178C and ED-12B/DO-178B. The documents listed in subparagraph 1.b provide guidance for establishing the software life cycle planning, development, verification, configuration management, quality assurance and certification liaison processes, in the form of objectives for the software life cycle processes, activities that provide a means of satisfying those objectives, and descriptions of the evidence indicating that they have been satisfied. | Statement |
| **4.b** | The technical content of the AMC is, as far as practicable, harmonised with FAA AC 20-115D, which is also based on ED-12C/DO-178C. | Statement |

### Using the documents, sections 5 to 8

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **5.a** | An applicant who has established software development assurance processes using ED-12B/DO-178B may continue to use those processes, including tool qualification processes, for new software development and certification projects, provided six criteria are met: the processes are shown to have no known process deficiencies; they were previously used to develop software used in a certified product at a software level at least as high as the software to be developed; where model-based development, object-oriented technology or formal methods are to be used, the existing processes for them were found acceptable by EASA on a previous certified project; where configuration data is used, the existing processes for it were found acceptable by EASA on a previous certified project; there are no significant changes to the software processes described in the plans or to the development environment; and the applicant does not intend to declare the software as having satisfied ED-12C/DO-178C. | Permitted |
| **5.b** | Where those criteria are not met, upgrade the processes and develop the new software using ED-12C/DO-178C, addressing tool qualification in accordance with Section 12.2 of ED-12C/DO-178C and paragraph 10 of the AMC. | Accepted method |
| **5.c** | Establish new software life cycle processes in accordance with ED-12C/DO-178C. | Accepted method |
| **6** | ED-12C/DO-178C is an acceptable means of compliance with regard to the software aspects of product certification or ETSO authorisation. | Accepted method |
| **6.a** | Satisfy all of the objectives associated with the software level assigned to the software, develop all of the associated life cycle data, and plan and execute activities that satisfy each objective, as listed in the Annex A tables of ED-12C/DO-178C and, where applicable, of ED-215/DO-330, ED-216/DO-333, ED-217/DO-332 and ED-218/DO-331. | Accepted method |
| **6.b** | Submit to EASA the life cycle data specified in Section 9.3 of ED-12C/DO-178C, and in Section 9.0 a. of ED-215/DO-330 as applicable to tool qualification. It is the applicant's responsibility to perform the planned activities and produce the life cycle data needed to satisfy all the applicable objectives. | Accepted method |
| **6.c** | Not all of the life cycle data related to the type design applies to all software levels: "the design description and the source code are not part of the type design data for Level D software". | Statement |
| **6.d** | Make available to EASA, upon request, any of the data described in Section 11 of ED-12C/DO-178C, the applicable tool qualification data, the data outputs from any applicable supplements, and any other data needed to substantiate satisfaction of all the applicable objectives. | Accepted method |
| **6.e** | EASA may publish an AMC to specific certification specifications, stating the required relationship between the criticality of the software-based systems and the software levels defined in ED-12C/DO-178C. Such an AMC "takes precedence over the application of Section 2.3 of ED-12C/DO-178C". | Statement |
| **7** | Section 7 is reserved. | Statement |
| **8.a** | Apply the guidance of the supplements ED-216/DO-333, ED-217/DO-332 and ED-218/DO-331 when incorporating the software development techniques they address. Where several techniques are used together, more than one supplement applies, and a supplement is not used as a stand-alone document. | Accepted method |
| **8.a** | Describe in the plan for software aspects of certification how ED-12C/DO-178C and the supplements are applied together, and which objectives from which documents apply to which software components. Where a technique addressed by a supplement is used to develop a qualified tool, describe in the tool qualification plan which tool qualification objectives the technique affects and how the planned activities satisfy them. | Accepted method |
| **8.a** | Where models are used as the basis for developing software, identify which review and analysis objectives are planned to be satisfied by simulation, alone or with reviews and analyses, satisfy all other objectives by reviews and analyses, and justify in detail for each identified objective how the simulation activity fully satisfies it. | Accepted method |
| **8.b** | Field-loadable software: provide the information needed to support the system-level guidance identified in ED-12C/DO-178C Section 2.5.5 and ED-12B/DO-178B Section 2.5; protect the software against corruption or partial loading at an integrity level appropriate for its software level; make the loaded part number verifiable by appropriate means; and implement protection mechanisms to prevent inadvertent enabling of the field-loading function during cruising or any other safety-critical phase. | Accepted method |
| **8.c** | User-modifiable software: provide the information needed to support the system-level guidance identified in ED-12C/DO-178C Section 2.5.2 and ED-12B/DO-178B Section 2.4; and develop the modifiable part of the software at a software level at least as high as the software level assigned to that software. | Accepted method |

### Legacy software and tools, sections 9 and 10

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **9.b** | Assess legacy software that is to be modified or reused for its usage history from previous installations. Where it has safety-related service difficulties, airworthiness directives or open problem reports with a potential safety impact, establish plans to resolve all related software deficiencies, and correct any related development process deficiencies before modifying or reusing it. | Accepted method |
| **9.b** | The system safety process assigns the minimum development assurance level, based on the severity classifications of failure conditions for a given function. Use Table 1 of the AMC to determine whether the legacy software level satisfies the software level assigned by that process for the proposed installation. | Accepted method |
| **9.b** | Where the legacy software level is not acceptable, upgrade the software development baseline, including all processes, procedures and tool qualification processes, using Section 12.1.4 of ED-12C/DO-178C and ED-215/DO-330, or, for ED-12B/DO-178B legacy software, of ED-12B/DO-178B or ED-12C/DO-178C and ED-215/DO-330. | Accepted method |
| **9.b** | Where the usage history and software level criteria are satisfied and no modification is required, the original approval may serve as the basis for the software in the installation approval of the proposed system. | Permitted |
| **9.b** | Where modifications are required, conduct a software change impact analysis to determine the extent and impact of the modifications and the verification required, conduct that verification, and summarise the results in the plan for software aspects of certification or in the software accomplishment summary. | Accepted method |
| **9.b** | An applicant who has upgraded the baseline to ED-12C/DO-178C and updated all processes, procedures and tool qualification processes may declare the software as equivalent to satisfying ED-12C/DO-178C. The applicant may not declare unmodified tools as equivalent to satisfying ED-12C/DO-178C and ED-215/DO-330. | Permitted |
| **9.b** | Where new software tools or modifications to tools are needed, determine the tool qualification requirements under paragraph 10 of the AMC. | Accepted method |
| **9.b** | An applicant may use existing processes to modify legacy software under the version of ED-12/DO-178 used for the original approval, provided that prior EASA acceptance exists for any model-based development, object-oriented technology or formal methods processes; that the software plans, processes and life cycle environment have been maintained and can still be used; and that the applicant does not intend to declare the software as satisfying ED-12C/DO-178C. | Permitted |
| **9.b** | Where those conditions are satisfied, all modifications may be accomplished using the same ED-12/DO-178 version as the original approval, but the software may not then be declared equivalent to satisfying ED-12C/DO-178C. Where configuration data is used, the existing processes for it may be used where EASA found them acceptable on a previous certified project; in the absence of such processes, establish new processes for parameter data items in accordance with ED-12C/DO-178C. | Permitted |
| **9.b** | Where any of those conditions is not satisfied, update all processes, procedures and tool qualification processes using ED-12C/DO-178C and ED-215/DO-330, and make all modifications to the software using Section 12.1 of ED-12C/DO-178C. | Accepted method |
| **10** | Sections 12.2 of ED-12C/DO-178C and ED-215/DO-330 provide an acceptable method for tool qualification. ED-215/DO-330 contains its own complete set of objectives, activities and life cycle data for tool qualification. | Statement |
| **10.a** | Where the legacy software was previously approved using ED-12/DO-178 or ED-12A/DO-178A and a new or modified tool is to be used for modifications to it, use the criteria of Section 12.2 of ED-12C/DO-178C to determine whether tool qualification is needed. Where it is, use the software level assigned by the system safety assessment to determine the required tool qualification level, and use ED-215/DO-330 for the applicable objectives, activities and life cycle data. The applicant may declare the qualified tool as satisfying ED-215/DO-330, but not the legacy software as equivalent to satisfying ED-12C/DO-178C. | Accepted method |
| **10.b** | Where the legacy software was previously approved using ED-12B/DO-178B and no equivalence to ED-12C/DO-178C is to be declared, the applicant can either use the ED-12B/DO-178B tool qualification processes to qualify new or modified tools, or update those processes and qualify the tool using ED-215/DO-330, referring to Table 2 of the AMC for the required tool qualification level, and may then declare the qualified tool as satisfying ED-215/DO-330. | Permitted |
| **10.c** | ED-12C/DO-178C establishes five levels of tool qualification, based on the tool use and its potential impact on the software life cycle processes, and does not address tools previously qualified to the ED-12B/DO-178B criteria. For such a tool, use Table 2 of the AMC to determine the correlation between the ED-12B/DO-178B tool qualification type and the ED-12C/DO-178C tool criteria and tool qualification levels. | Accepted method |
| **10.c** | For a development tool previously qualified using ED-12B/DO-178B whose assigned software level correlates with or exceeds the required tool qualification level, the ED-12B/DO-178B tool qualification processes may continue to be used, with a tool change impact analysis under Section 11.2.2 or 11.2.3 of ED-215/DO-330 where the tool or its operational environment changes. Where the assigned level does not satisfy the required tool qualification level, update the tool qualification processes and requalify the tool using ED-215/DO-330. | Accepted method |
| **10.c** | For a verification tool previously qualified using ED-12B/DO-178B where TQL-5 is required, the ED-12B/DO-178B tool qualification process may continue to be used, with a tool change impact analysis and reverification or requalification where the tool or its operational environment changes. Where TQL-4 is required, requalify the verification tool using ED-215/DO-330. | Accepted method |
| **10.c** | The applicant may declare a tool as equivalent to satisfying ED-215/DO-330 where all the changes to the tool and to the tool qualification processes satisfy ED-215/DO-330. | Permitted |
| **11** | Section 11 lists the related EASA certification specifications, including CS-27, CS-29 and CS-E, the related FAA advisory circulars, and the industry documents the AMC names. | Statement |
| **12** | EASA certification specifications and AMC are available at www.easa.europa.eu, and FAA advisory circulars at www.faa.gov. EUROCAE and RTCA documents are "available on payment" from their publishers. | Statement |

Section 9 also carries Figure 1, a flow chart for using legacy software. It is a
figure, and the vault does not restate a figure in words either. The AMC directs
the applicant to use the flow chart while following the procedures of section 9,
and to coordinate with EASA any case that does not follow it
[ext AMC 20-115D 9.b].

Table 1 and Table 2 are tables, and accuracy rule 6 keeps the vault from
restating a table in words. Table 1 maps an assigned software level of A, B, C
or D onto the legacy levels A, B, C and D of ED-12B, 1, 2 and 3 of ED-12A, and
Critical, Essential and Non-Essential of ED-12, and Table 2 maps an ED-12B
development or verification tool onto tool qualification levels TQL-1 to TQL-5.
Those are the software and tool level names the AMC itself uses; the mappings
between them are in the tables and are read there.

### Acceptable means

The AMC carries three pieces of guidance material of its own.

| Ref | Obligation | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **GM1** | A software change impact analysis identifies the released software baseline on which the proposed software is to be built, and provides a summary of the changes and their impact, a listing and description of the problem reports to be corrected and of the related change requests, and a listing of the new functions to be activated or implemented. | Statement |
| **GM1** | A change impact analysis addresses changes, where applicable, to the software level; the development or verification environment; the software processes; the tools; the processor or other hardware components and interfaces; the configuration data, especially when activating or deactivating functions; the software interface characteristics and input and output requirements; and the software requirements, design, architecture and code components, including the items affected by the change and not only the modified life cycle data. | Statement |
| **GM1** | For each applicable item, the analysis describes the resulting impact of the changes and identifies the activities to be performed to satisfy ED-12C/DO-178C or ED-12B/DO-178B and to continue to satisfy the requirements for safe operation. | Statement |
| **GM2** | Data coupling analysis is of a different type and purpose than control coupling analysis. Both analyses are necessary to satisfy objective A-7 (8) of ED-12C/DO-178C and ED-12B/DO-178B. | Required |
| **GM2** | Although they support a verification objective, data coupling and control coupling analyses rely on good practices in the software design phase, for example through the specification of the interfaces and of the dependencies between components. | Statement |
| **GM3** | Handle the foreseeable sources of software error at design level, rather than only at source code review level, to protect against foreseeable unintended software behaviour. | Accepted method |
| **GM3** | Reduce the possibility of unintended software behaviour by identifying the foreseeable sources of software errors, being runtime exceptions or errors such as fixed or floating-point arithmetic overflow, stack or heap overflow, division by zero, and counter or timer overrun or wrap-around; data or memory corruption and timing issues, such as those caused by a lack of partitioning or improper interrupt or cache management; and features leading to unpredictable programme execution, such as dynamic allocation, out-of-order execution or resource contention. | Accepted method |
| **GM3** | Identify the associated mitigation for each foreseeable source of error, and specify the protection mechanisms, including error-handling mechanisms, in the high-level or low-level software requirements. | Accepted method |
| **GM3** | For software Levels A and B, give consideration to incorporating runtime protection mechanisms, since reliance on probabilistic approaches or static analyses alone may not be appropriate. Implementing such mechanisms for the other software levels may be good practice. | Accepted method |
| **GM3** | The use of formal methods in accordance with ED-216/DO-333 may enhance the detection of runtime errors. | Permitted |

[VERIFY: unlisted construction. The GM2 row carries Required on "are necessary".
The phrasing is neither one of the seven source verbs nor a listed declaratory
form. The vault reads a statement of necessity as Required, as it reads "is
required to". [[AMC 20-3B]] records the same open question for its own rows, and
the owner decides the construction once for every row in the vault that carries
it.]

## Bearing on this engine

**The substance is in a document this vault does not hold, and never will.**
ED-12C/DO-178C, the supplements ED-215/DO-330, ED-216/DO-333, ED-217/DO-332 and
ED-218/DO-331, and the supporting ED-94C/DO-248C are sold by EUROCAE and by
RTCA, Inc., which the AMC states in the plainest terms: those documents are
"available on payment" [ext AMC 20-115D 12]. No paywalled material is committed
to this repository, so the objectives, the activities and the life cycle data
that define each software level are recorded nowhere here. The note above is the
whole of what AMC 20-115D says on its own authority. `review/dead_ends.md` lists
what that leaves unstated.

**What it does settle is which method is accepted.** [[CS-E 50|CS-E 50(f)]]
requires the software and the encoded logic to be developed by an approved
method consistent with the criticality of the functions performed, and names no
method. AMC 20-115D supplies one: ED-12C/DO-178C with its supplements, or, under
six stated conditions, an applicant's existing ED-12B/DO-178B processes
[ext AMC 20-115D 5.a]. [[AMC 20-3B]] closes the loop from the engine side, by
accepting methods compliant with the latest edition of AMC 20-115 for software.
Anything else is an alternative means, and it must be approved by EASA on a
product basis [ext AMC 20-115D 1.a].

**The engine is inside the applicability.** Section 2 reaches software to be
installed on type-certified aircraft, engines and propellers
[ext AMC 20-115D 2]. The engine declares a full-authority EECS, so its software
is part of the engine type design, its criticality level is determined by the
engine safety assessment of [[CS-E 510]], and the level is agreed with the
aircraft applicant before the certification activity — which is the duty
[[AMC 20-1A]] places on the installer's side of the same agreement.

**One EASA rule sits above the industry document.** Where EASA publishes an AMC
to a specific certification specification stating the required relationship
between the criticality of the software-based systems and the software levels,
that AMC "takes precedence over the application of Section 2.3 of
ED-12C/DO-178C" [ext AMC 20-115D 6.e]. This is the one place where the EASA text
displaces the document it recognises.

[VERIFY: whether EASA has published such an AMC for CS-E, fixing the required
relationship between engine function criticality and software level. CS-E 50(f)
asks only for a method consistent with the criticality of the functions
performed, and neither [[AMC E 50]] nor [[AMC 20-3B]] states a mapping from a
Hazardous or Major Engine Effect to a software level. If none exists,
Section 2.3 of ED-12C/DO-178C governs, and that section is in a document this
vault does not hold.]

[VERIFY: whether the EECS of this engine uses field-loadable software,
user-modifiable software, or software previously approved under ED-12/DO-178,
ED-12A/DO-178A or ED-12B/DO-178B. Sections 8.b, 8.c and 9 bind only in those
cases, and `engine_profile.md` declares the control system as EECS-FADEC without
stating how its software is loaded or where it comes from. The answer changes
what is owed: field-loadable software adds a loading protection and part number
duty that meets the configuration control provisions recorded in [[AMC 20-3B]],
and legacy software adds the change impact analysis of GM1.]
